AWS CloudFront - Handwritten Study Notes
AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 1
☁️ Amazon CloudFront — Content Delivery Network (CDN)

1. Introduction

In the previous section, we worked with:

  • Amazon EC2 — to host a website/application
  • Amazon S3 — to store website files and static content
  • Amazon Route 53 — for DNS and routing

Now we take the concept one level further.

🎯 The Next Challenge

Suppose your website is hosted in the Mumbai AWS Region.
If users from Europe access the website, their requests may need to travel a long distance to reach the Mumbai Region.

This can result in:

  • Higher latency
  • Longer loading time
  • Slower content delivery
  • Poorer user experience

Therefore, the next challenge is: How can we serve our website globally with low latency and better performance?

2. Two Approaches to Global Website Delivery

Suppose we want users around the world to access our website quickly.

Approach 1: Deploy Multiple EC2 Instances

We could deploy: One EC2 instance in Mumbai, another EC2 instance in Stockholm/Europe, and more instances in other regions. Then users could be served from a geographically closer region.

Users ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ Europe India ↓ ↓ Stockholm Mumbai EC2 EC2

❌ Problem

The more EC2 instances and AWS Regions we use:

  • The more resources we have to manage
  • The higher the infrastructure cost
  • The more complex the architecture becomes

Therefore, we need a more efficient solution.

3. ⭐ Solution: Amazon CloudFront

The solution is: Amazon CloudFront

Amazon CloudFront is a Content Delivery Network (CDN) provided by AWS.

Main Purpose

CloudFront helps: Deliver website content to users with lower latency and better performance.

Instead of every user directly accessing the original server, CloudFront can cache content at locations that are geographically closer to users.

4. What is a CDN?

CDN = Content Delivery Network

A CDN is a globally distributed network used to deliver content efficiently to users. Instead of serving every request from one central server, a CDN stores/caches frequently requested content at geographically distributed locations.

Without CDN:

User in Europe↓Internet↓Mumbai AWS Region↓S3/EC2

With CloudFront:

User in Europe↓Nearest CloudFront Edge Location↓Cached Content

This can significantly reduce the distance between the user and the content being served.

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 2

5. How CloudFront Works

CloudFront works using caching. Suppose your website contains: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Images, Videos, Other static files. CloudFront can cache suitable content at its distributed locations.

First Request

Suppose a user in Europe requests your website for the first time.

European User↓CloudFront Edge Location↓Cache Miss↓Origin (S3/EC2)↓Content returned↓Edge Location caches content↓User

The first request may need to go back to the origin.

6. Subsequent Requests

Now another user near the same CloudFront location requests the same cached content.

Second User↓CloudFront Edge Location↓Cache Hit↓Content delivered directly

The request does not necessarily need to go all the way back to the original S3 bucket or EC2 server.

⭐ Result

Lower latency | Faster content delivery | Better user experience | Reduced load on the origin

7. Origin

The origin is the original location from which CloudFront retrieves content. CloudFront can work with different types of origins.

Examples mentioned in the practical: Amazon S3, Elastic Load Balancer, API Gateway, Other supported origins.

CloudFront ↓ Origin ┌───────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ S3 EC2 ELB

8. What Does CloudFront Cache?  |  9. Dynamic Content

Static Content

CloudFront can cache content such as: Images, CSS files, JavaScript files, HTML, Videos, Other static website assets.

For example, instead of repeatedly downloading high-resolution images from the origin, CloudFront caches them closer to users.

9. Dynamic Content

CloudFront can cache certain dynamic content (HTML/API responses). However, sensitive, user-specific data and backend logic are generally not cached by default.

⚠️ Important

Avoid caching data that is: User-specific, Sensitive, Private, or Frequently changing in a way that could cause incorrect data to be served.

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 3

10. CloudFront Edge Locations

One of the most important CloudFront concepts is: Edge Location.

An Edge Location is a CloudFront location where content can be cached and served closer to users.

Example: Suppose users are located in India, Europe, North America, and Asia-Pacific. CloudFront has a globally distributed network of locations. Therefore, users can potentially receive content from a location closer to them.

11. Why Edge Locations Matter

Imagine your origin is located in Mumbai.

Without CloudFront:

User→Mumbai Origin

With CloudFront:

User→Nearest Edge Location→Cached Content

The physical/network distance can be reduced, improving delivery performance.

12. CloudFront vs Multiple EC2 Instances

This is an important architectural comparison.

Multiple EC2 Instances CloudFront
Deploy servers in multiple regions Distribute/cache content globally
More infrastructure Less need for multiple origin servers for cached content
Higher management complexity Managed CDN service
Can increase infrastructure cost Cost primarily depends on usage and configuration
Useful for globally distributed application compute Excellent for content delivery and caching
⭐ Important CloudFront does not simply replace multiple regional application servers in every situation. The correct solution depends on the application's architecture and requirements.

13. Practical — Website Deployment  |  14 & 15

The practical example uses a simple website containing index.html, images, etc. The website is first uploaded to an S3 bucket (e.g. my-website-312024).

14. Why Not Direct S3 Access?

The purpose is to make CloudFront the delivery layer. We want User → CloudFront → S3 instead of User → S3 directly.

15. Create a Distribution

A distribution defines how CloudFront should deliver content.

Origin Domain:

Choose the origin from which CloudFront will retrieve content. For this practical: Amazon S3 Bucket.

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 4

CloudFront Configuration (16 - 19)

16. Origin Access

CloudFront needs permission to access the S3 origin. The practical uses the recommended config, allowing CloudFront → S3 while users access content via CloudFront.

17. Cache Policy

Controls caching behavior: What can be cached, how requests are handled, how long content remains cached, and which request characteristics affect caching.

18. Price Class

Controls which CloudFront edge locations are used.

  • All Edge Locations: Broadest global coverage, best performance.
  • Selected regions: Potentially lower cost, restricted usage.

19. Default Root Object

Specifies which object is served when the root of the distribution is requested. For a website, we commonly specify: index.html

20. Create the Distribution  |  21. Domain Name

⚠️ Important CloudFront is a global service, so it is not treated like a normal Region-specific resource. The distribution may take some time to become fully deployed.

Once the distribution is created, CloudFront provides a domain name similar to: xxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net. This becomes the URL through which users can access the distribution.

User→CloudFront Domain Name→Edge Location→S3 Origin

22. Testing the Website  |  23. Performance Test

Open the CloudFront distribution domain name in a browser. The website should load through CloudFront.

First Request

May take longer because CloudFront may need to retrieve content from the origin (e.g. ~640 ms).

Subsequent Requests

After content is cached, subsequent requests may be faster (e.g. ~200 ms or ~195 ms).

Note Actual performance depends on user location, edge location, network conditions, object size, cache status, and origin performance.
AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 5

24. Cache Hit and Cache Miss

These two terms are extremely important.

Cache Hit

A requested object is already available in the CloudFront cache.

User↓Edge Location↓Object found↓CACHE HIT↓Content delivered

Result: Usually faster delivery.

Cache Miss

The requested object is not currently available in the cache.

User↓Edge Location↓Object not found↓CACHE MISS↓Origin → Content

25. CloudFront Monitoring  |  Cache Hit Ratio

CloudFront provides monitoring and statistics: Requests, Cache hits, Cache misses, Errors, Traffic.

Cache Hit Ratio: Represents how often requests can be served from cache instead of going to the origin. Generally: Higher cache hit ratio → less work for the origin and potentially faster content delivery.

26. CloudFront Architecture

The complete architecture can be visualized as:

GLOBAL USERS ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Europe India America │ │ │ └─────────┼─────────┘ ↓ CloudFront Edge Locations ↓ Cache / Delivery ↓ Origin ┌─────┴─────┐ ↓ ↓ S3 EC2

The key idea: Users are served through CloudFront, while CloudFront retrieves content from the origin when necessary.

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 6

27 & 28. CloudFront Terminology  |  POPs

27.1 Edge Location

A location in the CloudFront network used to serve content closer to users.

27.2 Regional Edge Cache

A larger intermediate caching layer. It can help reduce repeated trips to the origin when content is not available at a particular edge location.

User→Edge Location→Regional Cache→Origin

27.3 Point of Presence (POP)

A network location used to provide connectivity and content delivery services.

28. Embedded POPs

Can involve infrastructure associated with Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to improve network proximity/performance.

29. Browser Cache vs CloudFront Cache

Browser Cache

A browser can cache website content locally for an individual user.

Limitation:

The cache is generally associated with that user's browser. If User B accesses the website, they still need to retrieve content.

CloudFront Cache

CloudFront provides a shared, distributed caching layer.

User A ─┐ ├──→ CloudFront Edge Cache User B ─┤ │ User C ─┘

Allows cached content to be reused for multiple users.

30. CloudFront Pricing Concept

CloudFront pricing is primarily usage-based. The practical highlights that the edge locations themselves are not something you separately pay for simply because they exist.

Costs can depend on: Data transfer, Number of requests, Region/geography, Features used, Configuration. AWS also provides a CloudFront free-tier allowance (verify current pricing).

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 7

31. CloudFront vs Multi-Region Hosting

A common question is: Should I use CloudFront or deploy my application in multiple AWS Regions? There is no single answer. It depends on the use case.

Use CloudFront when:

  • You need global content delivery
  • Website contains lots of static assets
  • You want caching
  • You want lower content-delivery latency
  • You want to reduce repeated requests to the origin

Multi-Region Architecture when:

  • Application compute must exist close to users
  • You need regional application redundancy
  • You need active-active or active-passive regional architectures
  • The application itself requires region-level distribution
⭐ Best Concept CloudFront and multi-region architecture are not necessarily alternatives. They can be used together!
Users ↓ CloudFront / \ ↓ ↓ Region 1 Region 2 ↓ ↓ Application Application

32. Request Flow  |  33. CloudFront Cleanup

First Request Flow

User requests website → Request reaches CloudFront → CloudFront checks edge cache → Object not found → Cache Miss → CloudFront requests object from origin → Origin returns object → CloudFront caches content → Delivered to user.

Next Request

User requests same content → CloudFront checks edge cache → Object found → Cache Hit → Delivered directly.

33. Cleanup Rules

After completing a practical, resources should be cleaned up.

CloudFront Distribution:

Disable→Wait→Delete

S3 Bucket:

Delete Objects→Delete Bucket
AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 8

34. ⭐ Important Concepts to Remember

TermMeaning
CloudFrontAWS Content Delivery Network
CDNContent Delivery Network
OriginOriginal source of content
Edge LocationLocation where CloudFront can cache/serve content
Cache HitRequested content is available in cache
Cache MissRequested content is not available in cache
Regional Edge CacheIntermediate caching layer
POPPoint of Presence
DistributionCloudFront configuration used to deliver content
Default Root ObjectObject served for the distribution root, e.g. index.html
Cache PolicyControls caching behavior

35. ⭐ Key Benefits of CloudFront

  • 1. Low Latency: Delivered from locations closer to users.
  • 2. Faster Website: Cached content without hitting origin.
  • 3. Global Delivery: Distributed delivery network.
  • 4. Better UX: Faster loading improves experience.
  • 5. Reduced Origin Load: Cached requests save origin compute.
  • 6. Scalability: Efficiently handle large numbers of requests.

36. ⚠️ Important Practical Points

  • • CloudFront is a global AWS service.
  • • Original source is called the Origin (e.g. S3).
  • • EC2/app infra can also be behind CloudFront.
  • • Cache Hit = found in cache. Cache Miss = retrieve from origin.
  • • index.html can be the Default Root Object.
  • • The distribution may take time to deploy.
  • • Disable a distribution before deleting it.
  • • CF and multi-region hosting solve related but different problems.

37. 🧠 One-Minute Revision

What is CloudFront?

AWS's CDN that delivers content globally with lower latency by caching closer to users.

Origin vs Edge Location:

Origin = Original source. Edge Location = Where content is cached and delivered.

Why use it?

To improve global delivery performance, reduce latency, and reduce repeated origin requests.

AWS CERTIFIED CLOUD PRACTITIONER & SAA // STUDY NOTES PAGE 9

38. 🎯 Interview Questions

Q1. What is Amazon CloudFront?
An AWS CDN that distributes content through a global network to provide faster/lower-latency delivery.
Q2. Why do we need a CDN?
To deliver content from locations closer to users, reducing latency and improving performance.
Q3. What is an Edge Location?
A CloudFront location where content can be cached and served closer to users.
Q4. What is an Origin?
The original source from which CloudFront retrieves content (e.g. S3 bucket or EC2 application).
Q5. What is a Cache Hit?
Occurs when the requested content is already available at the cache and can be served from there.
Q6. What is a Cache Miss?
Occurs when the content is not available in the cache, requiring CloudFront to retrieve it from the origin.
Q7. Can CloudFront use S3 as an origin?
Yes, Amazon S3 can be configured as a CloudFront origin.
Q8. Can it work with an app on EC2?
Yes. CloudFront can be placed in front of application infra so suitable content is delivered via CDN.
Q9. Purpose of Default Root Object?
Specifies the default object to return when a user requests the root (e.g. index.html).
Q10. CF or multiple EC2 Regions?
Depends. CF is a delivery/caching layer. Multi-region distributes app infra. They can be used together.

🔥 Final Architecture to Remember

🌍 GLOBAL USERS / | \ / | \ Europe India USA \ | / \ | / ↓ ↓ ↓ ☁️ AMAZON CLOUDFRONT CDN ↓ Edge Locations ↓ Cache Layer ↓ Origin ┌─────┴─────┐ ↓ ↓ S3 EC2
💡 The Core Idea

Without CloudFront: User → Origin
With CloudFront: User → Nearest/appropriate CloudFront Edge → Cache → Origin when required

⭐ Remember This Line

Amazon CloudFront is used to deliver content globally with low latency by caching suitable content closer to users.

🚀 AWS Amplify — Detailed Notes

1. Introduction to AWS Amplify

AWS Amplify is a development platform that helps developers build, deploy, and host web and mobile applications using AWS services.

It simplifies many tasks that would otherwise require configuring multiple AWS services manually.

Amplify can help with:

  • Building & Deploying apps
  • Hosting websites
  • Continuous deployment
  • Custom domains & SSL/TLS
  • Authentication (Cognito)
  • APIs & Databases (DynamoDB)
  • Storage & Backend resources
  • Local development & Cloud Sandbox
Simple Definition

AWS Amplify simplifies the process of building, deploying, and hosting modern web and mobile applications on AWS.

Why Do We Need Amplify?

Creating a website is only one part of the process. Doing everything manually requires configuring several AWS services. Amplify simplifies this workflow:

Application→Deployment→Hosting→Custom Domain→SSL→HTTPS→Continuous Deployment

The first practical example uses a simple static website stored in GitHub.

my-repository/ │ ├── index.html └── styles.css

  2. Create/Deploy an application
  3. Select Source (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)

One of the most useful features is continuous deployment.

Suppose the website is deployed. You edit index.html locally (e.g. changing text from V7 to V8) and push the commit to GitHub.

The Automation Flow

⭐ Key Concept Git commit → Amplify build → Automatic deployment → Updated website. You do not have to manually upload files again!

Amplify provides a clear view of deployment history. You can view: Deployment status, previous builds, commit information, and build details. This is vital for tracing when and why a deployment occurred.

A production website needs a custom domain (e.g. example.com) instead of the default Amplify URL. In Amplify, go to Hosting → Custom domains to add it.

If using Amazon Route 53:

User ↓ Frontend (React / Angular) ↓ API ↓ Backend ↓ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Database Authentication Storage (DynamoDB) (Cognito) (S3) ↑ | (Lambda)

Implementing auth, databases, and APIs manually from scratch is huge work (registration, passwords, security, infrastructure scaling). Amplify simplifies integration with managed services:

Docker - Detailed & Structured Handwritten Notes
DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 1
🐳 Docker — Detailed & Structured Notes

1. What is Docker?

Docker is a containerization platform/tool used to create, manage, package, and run applications inside containers.

It is especially useful for developers because it simplifies the complete application lifecycle, including:

  • Application development
  • Packaging
  • Testing
  • Shipping
  • Deployment
  • Running applications

Docker is very popular because it allows applications to run in an isolated and consistent environment.

Simple Definition

Docker packages an application together with the dependencies and configuration it needs so that it can run consistently in different environments.

2. Why Do We Need Docker?

One of the most common problems in software development is:

“It works on my machine, but it doesn't work on yours.”

Example

Suppose a developer creates an application. The application depends on: Node.js, Python, Database, Libraries, Dependencies, Configuration files, Environment variables, External services, and Specific software versions.

The developer successfully runs the application on their computer. Everything works perfectly. Now the testing team receives the application and tries to run it. But the application does not work.

The developer says: “The application is working fine on my machine.”

Why does this happen?

Because the developer's and tester's environments may be different. For example:

Developer EnvironmentTester Environment
Node.js v14Node.js v16
Required library installedLibrary missing
Correct configurationDifferent configuration
Required environment variablesMissing variables
Required dependency versionDifferent dependency version
Required service versionDifferent service version

These differences can create compatibility issues.

3. Docker as a Solution

Docker solves this problem by allowing the developer to package the application together with everything required to run it.

The package can contain: Application code, Dependencies, Libraries, Required tools, Configuration, Required runtime, Other necessary components.

The developer can then provide this package to the testing team. The tester only needs a Docker environment to run the package.

DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 2

Result

Instead of manually configuring everything again:

Developer→Package app + dependencies→Tester

The same packaged environment can be used across different machines.

⭐ Main Idea

Docker helps create a consistent environment for: Development → Testing → Deployment → Production

4. What is a Container?

A container is an isolated environment in which an application runs together with the dependencies it needs.

Think about a real-world shipping container. A shipping container: Holds goods, Keeps them together, Makes transportation easier, Can be moved from one place to another, Is isolated from other containers.

Docker containers work on a similar concept. A Docker container packages an application and the components required to run it.

5. Real-Life Container Analogy

Imagine that you need to transport something that must remain in a very cold environment.

Required item + Temperature control + Facilities

The container maintains the required environment while the item is transported. Similarly, a Docker container provides an isolated environment for an application.

Multiple Containers

You can have multiple containers on the same system:

+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | Container 1 | | Container 2 | | Container 3 | | Application A | | Application B | | Application C | +-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+

Each container provides isolation for its application.

6. Definition of Container

A container can be understood as:

A lightweight, isolated runtime environment that packages an application together with the dependencies and configuration required to run it.

Benefits of Containers:

  • Isolation
  • Portability
  • Consistency
  • Easy deployment
  • Easy sharing
  • Efficient resource usage
  • Faster application delivery

7. Docker Architecture

A simplified Docker environment can be represented as:

+--------------------------------------+ | Hardware | | Server / Desktop / Laptop / Cloud | +--------------------------------------+ ↓ +--------------------------------------+ | Operating System | | Linux / Windows etc. | +--------------------------------------+ ↓ +--------------------------------------+ | Docker Engine | | Manages Docker Containers | +--------------------------------------+ ↓ +-----------+-----------+ ↓ ↓ ↓ +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ |Container 1| |Container 2| |Container 3| | App 1 | | App 2 | | App 3 | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+

Docker Engine

Docker Engine is the core technology responsible for creating and managing containers. It allows us to: Create containers, Run containers, Stop containers, Manage containers, Work with Docker images.

DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 3

8. How Containers Reduce Compatibility Problems

Suppose an application requires: Application + Node.js 14 + Libraries + Dependencies + Configuration.

All of these requirements can be packaged into a Docker image and used to create a container. Therefore, when the application is moved to another environment, the required components travel with it.

Without Docker

Application↓Different Environment↓Compatibility Problems↓Application may fail

With Docker

App + Dependencies + Config↓Docker Image↓Container↓Run Application

9. Running Multiple Versions on the Same Machine

Another important benefit of containers is that multiple versions of software can be used independently.

Example

Suppose one application requires: Node.js 14 and another application requires: Node.js 16. Without isolation, managing different versions can become difficult. With Docker:

Machine │ ├── Container 1 │ ├── Application 1 │ └── Node.js 14 │ └── Container 2 ├── Application 2 └── Node.js 16

The applications can run in separate containers with their required environments.

⭐ Important Containers provide isolation, so applications can have different dependencies or runtime versions without directly interfering with each other.

10. Docker vs Virtual Machines

Docker containers and Virtual Machines (VMs) both provide isolation, but they work differently.

Docker Containers

Containers generally share the host operating system's kernel and isolate application processes. They package: Application, Dependencies, Required runtime/environment. They do not generally package a complete guest operating system for every application.

Virtual Machines

A VM virtualizes a complete machine and normally includes: Virtual hardware, Guest operating system, Libraries, Applications.

Simplified Comparison

Virtual Machines Hardware ↓ Host OS ↓ Hypervisor ↓ +-------------+ +-------------+ | VM 1 | | VM 2 | | Guest OS | | Guest OS | | Application | | Application | +-------------+ +-------------+
Docker Hardware ↓ Operating System ↓ Docker Engine ↓ +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ |Container 1| |Container 2| |Container 3| |Application| |Application| |Application| +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+

Key Differences

FeatureDocker ContainerVirtual Machine
IsolationProcess/application levelFull machine/OS level
Guest OS per instanceUsually noYes
Resource usageGenerally lowerGenerally higher
StartupGenerally fasterGenerally slower
PortabilityHighHigh
PackagingApp + dependenciesFull OS + app
Multiple versionsEasyPossible but heavier

⭐ Key Point: Containers are generally more lightweight because they don't require a complete guest operating system for every application.

DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 4

11. Main Components of Docker

The important Docker terms are:

  • Dockerfile
  • Docker Image
  • Docker Container
  • Docker Registry
  • Docker Hub
  • Docker Repository

The basic relationship is:

Dockerfile↓ BuildDocker Image↓ RunDocker Container↓Application

For sharing images:

Docker Image→Push→Docker Registry→Pull→Another Server

12. What is a Dockerfile?

A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions used to build a Docker image. It describes things such as: Base image, Working directory, Files to copy, Dependencies to install, Ports to expose, Commands to execute, Application startup command.

Example Dockerfile

FROM node:20 WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm install COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["npm", "start"]

Explanation

FROM: Specifies the base image (e.g. Node.js environment).

WORKDIR: Sets the working directory.

COPY: Copies files from the project into the image.

RUN: Executes a command while building the image.

EXPOSE: Documents the port the app uses.

CMD: Default command to run when container starts.

13. Docker Image  |  14. Image vs Container

A Docker image is a packaged, immutable template containing the application and the components required to create and run a container. It can contain: Application code, Runtime, Libraries, Dependencies, Configuration required by the image, Other required files.

Dockerfile→docker build→Docker Image

14. Image vs Container (Very Important)

Docker Image

An image is a template/package.

Docker Container

A container is a running instance of an image.

Docker Image │ ├──── Run → Container 1 │ ├──── Run → Container 2 │ └──── Run → Container 3
Easy Analogy Image = Blueprint | Container = Actual running building created from that blueprint
DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 5

15. Docker Registry  |  16. Docker Hub

15. Docker Registry

A Docker Registry is a storage and distribution system for Docker images. It allows images to be: Stored, Shared, Uploaded, Downloaded, Distributed. There can be public registries and private registries.

Developer→Build→Push→Registry→Pull→Another Dev/Server

16. Docker Hub

Docker Hub is a popular public Docker registry provided by Docker. It contains many publicly available container images. (e.g. Node.js, Python, MongoDB, Nginx, Redis, Ubuntu, MySQL).

Instead of creating from scratch:

docker pull node

This downloads a Node image from a registry such as Docker Hub.

17. Public vs Private  |  18. Registry vs Repository

17. Public vs Private Registries

Public Registry: Images are available publicly, subject to access rules (e.g. Docker Hub). Useful for sharing with the wider community.

Private Registry: Used to store images that should not be publicly accessible (e.g. Proprietary applications, Internal services, Private code).

18. Registry vs Repository

Registry: The larger image storage/distribution service (e.g. Docker Hub).

Repository: A collection of related images, commonly organized around an image/app name and its versions or tags.

Docker Hub (Registry) │ ├── node (Repository) │ ├── node:18 │ └── node:20 │ └── nginx (Repository) └── nginx:latest

Registry = Library | Repo = Section | Tag = Edition

19. Important Docker Commands

19.1 docker pull
Used to download an image from a registry. docker pull node:20

19.2 docker run
Used to create and start a container from an image. docker run node

19.3 docker build
Used to build an image from a Dockerfile. docker build -t my-image .
(-t names the image, . uses current directory)

19.4 docker ps
Shows running containers. docker ps (Add -a to see stopped ones too).

19.5 docker stop
Stops a running container. docker stop my-container

19.6 docker images
Lists Docker images available locally. docker images

20. Complete Workflow  |  21. Dockerfile → Image → Container

Developer writes application ↓ Dockerfile ↓ docker build ↓ Docker Image ↓ docker run ↓ Docker Container ↓ Application runs

21. The Crucial Relationship

Step 1: Dockerfile (Contains instructions)

Step 2: docker build (Docker reads Dockerfile)

Step 3: Image (The Docker image is created)

Step 4: docker run (Run the image)

Step 5: Container (A running instance is created)

DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 6

22. Multiple Containers  |  23. Important Benefits

22. Multiple Containers from One Image

Docker Image │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Container 1 Container 2 Container 3

The same application image could be used to start multiple instances of an application to handle more workload.

23. Important Benefits of Docker

  • Consistency: Dev → Test → Prod
  • Portability: Move between environments
  • Isolation: Apps run isolated
  • Efficient: More lightweight than VMs
  • Easy Deployment & Sharing: Package once, share via registries
  • Dependency Mgmt: Packaged with app
  • Multiple Versions: Different containers can use different dependency versions safely

24. Compatibility  |  25. SDLC  |  26. VM vs Docker Revision

24. Compatibility: Docker packages the Application + Dependencies into a Docker Image. The tester machine runs the exact same packaged environment, significantly reducing environment-related compatibility problems.

25. Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC): Docker maintains consistency across: Development → Build → Package → Testing → Deployment → Production.

DockerVM
Container-basedMachine virtualization
LightweightComparatively heavier
Shares host OS kernelIncludes complete guest OS per instance
Packages app + dependenciesPackages full OS + app
Generally faster startupGenerally slower startup
Efficient resource utilizationHigher resource requirements
🧠 Remember VM → Full machine environment | Container → Application environment

27 & 28. Terminology & One-Line Definitions

Docker: Platform/toolset for containerized application development and management.

Container: Isolated runtime environment containing an app and its required dependencies.

Dockerfile: Text file containing instructions to build a Docker image.

Docker Image: Packaged template containing the app and its required runtime components, used to create containers.

Docker Engine: Core technology that manages containers and images.

Docker Registry: Storage/distribution system for container images.

Docker Hub: Popular public Docker registry.

Repository: Collection of related container images (e.g. node, python).

Tag: Identifier distinguishing image variants/versions.

DOCKER & CONTAINERIZATION // STUDY NOTES PAGE 7

29. 🧠 Quick Revision — Docker in 60 Seconds

DOCKERFILE │ │ docker build ↓ DOCKER IMAGE │ │ docker run ↓ DOCKER CONTAINER │ ↓ APPLICATION
For sharing: IMAGE │ │ docker push ↓ REGISTRY │ │ docker pull ↓ OTHER MACHINE

30. ⭐ Most Important Points

  • Docker is used for containerization. Containers provide isolated environments.
  • Docker helps reduce environment and compatibility problems.
  • A Dockerfile contains instructions to build an image.
  • A Docker image is used to create containers. A container is a running instance of an image.
  • One image can be used to create multiple containers.
  • Docker containers are generally more lightweight than VMs.
  • Docker images can be stored and distributed through registries (e.g. Docker Hub).
  • A repository contains related images/tags.
  • docker build → builds an image. docker run → creates/starts a container.

31. 🎯 Interview Questions

Q1. What is Docker?
Docker is a containerization platform used to package, deploy, and run applications in isolated environments.
Q2. Why is Docker used?
To provide consistent application environments, reduce compatibility problems, simplify deployment, and improve portability.
Q3. What is a container?
An isolated runtime environment in which an application runs with its required dependencies.
Q4. What is a Dockerfile?
A text file containing instructions used to build a Docker image.
Q5. What is a Docker image?
A packaged template containing the application and components required to create and run containers.
Q6. Image vs Container?
An image is a template/package, while a container is a running instance created from that image.
Q7. Can one image create multiple containers?
Yes. The same image can be used to create multiple container instances.
Q8. What is Docker Hub?
A popular public registry for storing and distributing container images.
Q9. What is a Docker registry?
A system for storing and distributing container images.
Q10. Registry vs Repository?
A registry is the broader image storage/distribution service, while a repository is a collection of related images/tags within a registry.
Q11. Docker vs VM?
Docker containers generally share the host OS kernel and package the application environment, while a VM normally includes a complete guest operating system.
📌 Final Cheat Sheet
DOCKER │ Containerization │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ │ │ Dockerfile Docker Engine │ │ docker build │ ↓ │ Docker Image │ │ │ docker run │ ↓ │ Docker Container ←───────┘ │ ↓ Application
Image Distribution Developer │ ↓ Docker Image │ │ push ↓ Registry │ │ pull ↓ Other Developer / Server │ ↓ Container

The easiest way to remember:
Dockerfile builds the Image → Image creates the Container → Container runs the Application.
Registry stores/distributes Images → Docker Hub is a popular public Registry.

SSL & TLS - Handwritten Study Notes
CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 1
🔐 SSL & TLS — Detailed and Structured Notes

1. What is SSL/TLS?

SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS (Transport Layer Security) are cryptographic protocols used to secure communication between a client and a server over a network such as the Internet.

Their main purpose is to protect sensitive information while it is being transmitted.

Example: Internet Banking

Your Computer / Browser ↓ Internet ↓ Banking Website / Server

You may send sensitive information such as: Username, Password, Account-related info, Confidential data.

If communication is not properly secured, an attacker could potentially intercept the data. SSL/TLS helps protect this communication.

2. SSL vs TLS

SSL

Secure Sockets Layer

It is the older protocol family.

TLS

Transport Layer Security

TLS is the successor to SSL and is the protocol used by modern secure connections.

🧠 Remember

People still commonly say “SSL certificate” or “SSL connection”. However, modern HTTPS connections generally use TLS, not the old SSL protocols.

SSL → Older protocol
TLS → Successor and modern protocol

3. HTTPS and the Lock Icon

When you visit a website using HTTPS, the browser indicates that the connection is protected (e.g., https://example.com).

Browsers commonly show a lock icon. Inspecting the connection reveals:

  • Connection security
  • Certificate information
  • Certificate validity
  • Certificate issuer

What does HTTPS mean?
HTTPS = HTTP Secure. It uses TLS to protect HTTP communication between the client and server.

4. What Does SSL/TLS Provide?

SSL/TLS is designed to provide important security properties for communication. The three major concepts are:

Confidentiality Integrity Authentication

These concepts are extremely important for understanding secure communication.

CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 2

5. Confidentiality

Meaning: Confidentiality means that sensitive information should only be accessible to authorized parties.

Example

Imagine a confidential examination paper being transferred from a printing facility to an examination center. Only the authorized center should be able to access the contents. Someone who intercepts the transfer should not understand the contents.

Original Data ↓ Encryption ↓ Encrypted Data (Internet) ↓ Decryption ↓ Original Data

6. Integrity

Meaning: Ensuring that data has not been modified or tampered with during transmission.

Suppose the original examination paper is: DEMO

If an attacker changes it to: MO, the receiver should be able to detect that the data was modified.

Hashing and message authentication mechanisms can help detect such changes.

7. Authentication

Meaning: Verifying the identity of the party you are communicating with.

For example, when you visit a banking website, you want to know: “Am I actually communicating with the legitimate website?” Digital certificates help establish this identity.

8. Confidentiality, Integrity & Authentication

Security Property Main Question Common Mechanism
Confidentiality Can unauthorized people read the data? Encryption
Integrity Was the data modified? Hash / MAC-based integrity mechanisms
Authentication Who am I communicating with? Digital Certificates
🧠 Easy Memory Trick: CIA

C → Confidentiality
I → Integrity
A → Authentication

9. Encryption  |  10. Plaintext and Ciphertext

Encryption is the process of converting readable information (plaintext) into an encoded form (ciphertext) so that unauthorized parties cannot understand it.

Plaintext

The original readable message. Example: DEMO

Ciphertext

The encrypted version of the message. The exact output depends on the encryption algorithm and key.

CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 3

11. Simple Encryption Example

Imagine a very basic historical technique where every character is shifted by three positions (Caesar Cipher style).

D → G E → H M → P O → R
DEMO (Plaintext) ↓ Encryption GHPR (Ciphertext) ↓ Decryption DEMO
⚠️ Important

This is only a simple educational example. Modern TLS does not use this type of simple character-shifting encryption. Modern cryptography uses mathematically designed algorithms and cryptographic keys.

12. Types of Encryption

The two major categories discussed are:

Symmetric Encryption Asymmetric Encryption

13. Symmetric Encryption

In symmetric encryption, the same secret key is used for both encryption and decryption.

Same Secret Key │ ↓ Plaintext → Encryption → Ciphertext │ ↓ Decryption │ ↓ Plaintext

Advantages

  • Fast and Efficient
  • Suitable for large amounts of bulk data
  • Lower computational overhead

Main Challenge

Key distribution: How do you securely share the secret key between the two parties? If intercepted, an attacker can decrypt the communication.

14. Asymmetric Encryption

Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys: a Public Key and a Private Key.

General Concept

Public Key ↓ Encryption Private Key ↓ Decryption

Public Key: Can generally be shared openly.
Private Key: Must be kept secret by its owner.

Server ┌─────────────┐ │ Public Key │ ← Can be shared │ Private Key │ ← Must remain secret └─────────────┘
CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 4

15. Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption

Feature Symmetric Asymmetric
Keys Same secret key Public + private key pair
Speed Faster Generally slower
Computational cost Lower Higher
Large data Suitable Generally not preferred
Main challenge Key distribution Public key can be shared
Typical purpose Bulk data encryption Key exchange / authentication

16. Why Hybrid Encryption is Used

Instead of using only one, secure communication protocols combine their strengths. This idea is called hybrid cryptography/encryption.

Asymmetric Cryptography ↓ Secure Key Establishment ↓ Symmetric Session Key ↓ Fast Bulk Data Encryption ↓ Secure Communication

17. Example of Hybrid Encryption

Client Server │ │ │ ← Public-key mechanism →│ │ Establish secret │ │ session key │ │ │ │==== Symmetric Key ======│ │ Encrypted application │ │ data │ │========================>│

18. Common Encryption Algorithms

Symmetric Algorithms

Examples: AES, 3DES, RC4

Important: RC4 and 3DES are obsolete/unsuitable for modern deployments. AES is widely used.

Asymmetric Algorithms

Examples: RSA, DSA, ECDSA

Modern TLS uses elliptic-curve mechanisms (ECDSA, ECDHE) depending on config.

19. What is Hashing?  |  20. Example

Hashing is the process of converting input data into a fixed-length output called a hash value or digest.

Input Data↓Hash Function↓Fixed-Length Hash

Example

Input: DEMO → Hash Function → Same Hash.

Input: MODIFIED → Hash Function → Different Hash.

A small change in input produces a completely different digest.

CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 5

21. Fixed-Length Hash  |  22. Hashing and Integrity

One important property of cryptographic hash functions is that the output has a fixed size.

Small Input → SHA-256 → 256-bit digest Large Input → SHA-256 → 256-bit digest

Hashing can be used to detect whether data has changed.

Sender: Hash(Message) = H1

Receiver: Hash(Received Msg) = H2

If H1 == H2, data is consistent.

⚠️ Important

A plain hash alone does not prove who sent the message. An attacker could modify both the message and the hash. That is why authentication mechanisms such as MACs, digital signatures, and TLS's authenticated record protection are needed.

23. MD5  |  24. SHA

MD5

Message-Digest Algorithm 5.
Produces a 128-bit digest.

Considered cryptographically broken. Do not use for modern security purposes.

SHA (Secure Hash Algorithms)

Common SHA-2 variants:
SHA-256 → 256-bit digest
SHA-384 → 384-bit digest
SHA-512 → 512-bit digest

SHA-256 is commonly used in modern systems.

25. MAC  |  26. HMAC

A MAC (Message Authentication Code) is used to provide message integrity and authentication using a shared secret key.

HMAC = Hash-based Message Authentication Code. It combines a cryptographic hash function with a secret key.

Message + Secret Key ↓ HMAC ↓ Authentication Tag

Why is HMAC stronger than an ordinary hash?

Because the secret key is involved. An attacker without the secret key cannot simply modify the message and calculate a valid HMAC.

27. Hash vs HMAC

Hash HMAC
No secret key required Uses a secret key
Produces a digest Produces an authentication tag
Useful for integrity-related checks Provides integrity + authentication with a shared secret
Example: SHA-256 Example: HMAC-SHA-256
🧠 Remember Hash = Data → Digest  |  HMAC = Data + Secret Key → Authentication Tag
CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 6

28. Digital Certificates

A digital certificate helps a browser verify the identity associated with a website's public key. When you visit a secure website, the browser inspects its certificate.

The certificate contains: Website/domain identity, Public key, Issuer, Validity period, Digital signature.

29. What is a Certificate Authority (CA)?

A Certificate Authority is a trusted organization/entity that issues digital certificates.

Website Owner ↓ Requests Certificate ↓ Certificate Authority (CA) ↓ Verifies information & Issues Digital Certificate

The browser/OS has a set of trusted root certificate authorities. This system helps the browser determine whether a certificate chain can be trusted.

30 & 31. What Does a Certificate Contain?

  • 1. Subject: Identifies the entity/domain covered.
  • 2. Public Key: Contains the associated public key.
  • 3. Issuer: Identifies the CA that issued it.
  • 4. Validity Period: Valid from & Valid until.
  • 5. Digital Signature: CA digitally signs it.
  • 6. Signature Algorithm: Used for the signature.
Subject: example.com Issuer: Trusted CA Valid From: Date A Valid Until: Date B Public Key: Available Signature: Available

32. Certificate Authentication  |  33. Private Key

32. Validation Checks

The browser checks:

  • Within validity period?
  • Matches requested domain?
  • Issuing CA trusted?
  • Certificate chain valid?
  • Signature valid?
  • Revoked?

33. Private Key Protection

A certificate contains the public key. The private key is kept securely by the server and is not included in the certificate.

If an attacker obtains the private key, security is seriously compromised.

34-37. Trust, Issuers, Expiry & Formats

34. Trust Model: Root CA → Intermediate CA → Server Certificate.

35. Expiration: Certificates expire and must be renewed regularly.

36. Issuers: DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Sectigo, GlobalSign, etc.

37. Formats: PEM (Text-based), DER, PKCS#12/PFX.
PEM Example: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- ... -----END CERTIFICATE-----

CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 7

The TLS Handshake (Steps 38 - 44)

The overall TLS connection process establishes a secure connection between Client and Server.

Step 1 — ClientHello

Client sends supported TLS versions, cipher suites, and random/key-exchange info.

Step 2 — ServerHello

Server responds and selects compatible parameters for the connection.

Step 3 — Server Certificate

Server sends its digital certificate (containing public key and identity) to the client.

Step 4 — Certificate Verification

Browser validates the certificate chain. If valid, server identity is trusted.

Step 5 — Key Establishment

Client and server establish shared secret keying material (Modern TLS 1.3 commonly uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman like ECDHE for forward secrecy).

Step 6 — Session Keys

Handshake produces symmetric session keys used to protect the connection.

Step 7 — Secure Communication

Application data is protected using efficient symmetric cryptography and authenticated encryption/integrity mechanisms.

45. Simplified TLS Workflow

┌──────────────────────┐ │ Client / Browser │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ │ ClientHello ↓ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Server │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ │ ServerHello │ Certificate ↓ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Certificate │ │ Verification │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ↓ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Key Establishment │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ↓ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Session Keys │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ↓ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Secure Communication │ └──────────────────────┘
CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 8

46. How the Three Security Goals Are Achieved

Confidentiality: Provided through encryption (Plaintext → Encryption → Protected Data).

Integrity: Cryptographic integrity protection detects modifications (e.g., AEAD modes like AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).

Authentication: The server's certificate helps authenticate identity.

48. Important Terms at a Glance

TermMeaning
SSL / TLSSSL is older; TLS is the modern successor.
HTTPSHTTP protected using TLS.
Symmetric / Asymmetric KeySymmetric = Shared secret | Asymmetric = Public/Private pair
Hash / MAC / HMACHash = Digest | MAC/HMAC = Auth/Integrity with secret key
Digital Certificate / CABinds identity to public key | CA issues/signs it
Cipher SuiteSet of crypto algorithms used by TLS
TLS HandshakeProcess to negotiate parameters, authenticate & establish keys

49. Symmetric vs Asymmetric vs Hashing

Feature Symmetric Asymmetric Hashing
Main purpose Confidentiality (bulk) Key establishment, Auth Integrity / fingerprint
Keys Shared secret Public + private No key (for ordinary hash)
Reversible? Yes, with key Depends on operation No practical reversal
Speed Fast Slower Fast
Example AES RSA, ECDHE, ECDSA SHA-256

Comparisons (50 - 52)

50. Hash vs Encryption

Encryption: Designed to be reversible with key (Protect secrecy).

Hashing: One-way function (Produce data fingerprint).

51 & 52. Keys & Passwords

Cert vs Public Key: Cert is a signed document that contains the public key.

Private Key vs Password: Password is user-chosen. Private Key is mathematical secret for crypto pairs.

CYBERSECURITY & NETWORKING // STUDY NOTES PAGE 9

56. 🎯 Interview Questions

Q1. What is SSL?
Secure Sockets Layer. An older crypto protocol to secure network communication.
Q2. What is TLS?
Transport Layer Security. The successor to SSL, used for modern secure internet communication.
Q4. Three major security properties of TLS?
Confidentiality, Integrity, Authentication.
Q6. What is symmetric encryption?
Uses the same shared secret key for encryption and decryption.
Q7. What is asymmetric cryptography?
Uses a public/private key pair for key establishment and digital signatures.
Q10. What is hybrid encryption?
Combines public-key cryptography (for key establishment) with symmetric cryptography (for fast bulk data protection).
Q11. What is hashing?
Converts input data into a fixed-length digest.
Q13. What is HMAC?
Keyed message authentication mechanism combining a secret key with a hash function.
Q14. What is a digital certificate?
Binds an identity/domain to a public key and is digitally signed by a CA.
Q17. What happens in a TLS handshake?
Negotiate crypto parameters, server authenticates via certificate, establish shared session keys.

58. ⭐ Super-Important Cheat Sheet

TLS │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Confidentiality Integrity Authentication │ │ │ Encryption Integrity Certificate Protection │ ↓ Public Key + Identity

SYMMETRIC

Same Secret Key → Fast → Bulk Data (AES)

ASYMMETRIC

Public + Private Key → Key Estab/Signatures (RSA/ECDHE)

HASHING

Data → Hash Function → Fixed Digest (SHA-256)

HMAC

Message + Secret Key → Authentication Tag

🔥 Final TLS Flow to Remember

The easiest sentence to remember:
"TLS authenticates the server, establishes shared cryptographic keys, and then protects application data using efficient symmetric cryptography."

NGINX - Handwritten Study Notes
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 1
⚙️ NGINX — Detailed & Structured Notes

1. What is NGINX?

NGINX (pronounced "Engine-X") is a web server used to serve and deliver web content to users.

However, it is not limited to being just a web server. It can also work as a:

  • Reverse Proxy
  • Load Balancer
  • Caching Server
  • HTTP/HTTPS Server
  • TCP/UDP Proxy (with stream config)
⭐ Key Point

NGINX = Web Server + Reverse Proxy + Load Balancer + Caching + More

2. What is a Web Server?

A web server is software that receives requests from clients (usually web browsers) and sends back web content.

Basic Flow

User / Browser ↓ Internet ↓ Web Server ↓ Website Files (HTML/CSS/JS) ↓ Response ↓ User / Browser

3. Why Do We Need NGINX?

If you create index.html and style.css, how does a user access them? NGINX receives the HTTP request and returns the requested files based on its configuration.

4. Practical Setup  |  5. Launching an EC2 Instance

To practice, you need a server. An AWS EC2 instance is perfect.

  • Step 1: Give instance a name (e.g., nginx-server)
  • Step 2: Select OS (Amazon Linux)
  • Step 3: Configure Key Pair for SSH

Step 4: Network Access

AWS Security Groups act as a virtual firewall. To view an HTTP site, you MUST allow TCP Port 80.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 2

6 - 9. Installing and Managing NGINX

Connect to your EC2 server using EC2 Instance Connect or SSH. Since the default user isn't root, use sudo for admin commands.

# Install on Amazon Linux sudo yum install nginx -y # Start the service sudo systemctl start nginx # Check status sudo systemctl status nginx
CommandPurpose
sudo systemctl start nginxStart NGINX
sudo systemctl stop nginxStop NGINX
sudo systemctl restart nginxRestart NGINX (full stop/start)
sudo systemctl reload nginxReload configuration smoothly
sudo systemctl enable nginxStart automatically at boot

10. Accessing  |  11. IP Address and Port

If installed correctly, entering http://<PUBLIC-IP> in your browser will show the default NGINX welcome page.

Important Ports

HTTP → Port 80

HTTPS → Port 443

An IP Address + Port identifies exactly where a network service is listening.

12. How the HTTP Request Works

Browser ↓ HTTP Request Public IP : 80 ↓ NGINX ↓ Website Content → HTTP Response → Browser
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 3

13. NGINX Configuration  |  14. Structure

The main NGINX config file is typically located at: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

The configuration is organized into hierarchical blocks:

events { ... } http { server { location / { ... } } }

Blocks Breakdown (15 - 18)

15. events

Handles connection processing. Can be empty for basic setups: events {}. (Make sure it's plural!)

16. http

Contains all HTTP traffic configs: server blocks, logging, MIME types.

17. server

Defines how to handle requests for a specific virtual server/site. Contains listen, server_name, etc.

18. location

Determines how requests for specific URI paths (e.g., / or /about/) are processed.

19. listen  |  20. root

listen 80;
Tells NGINX to listen for HTTP traffic on port 80. You can change this to 8080 or 443.

root /usr/share/nginx/html;
Tells NGINX the physical directory on the server where the website files are stored.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 4

22. Creating Your Own Website

Before editing nginx.conf, always create a backup!

sudo cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.backup

23. Minimal NGINX Configuration

events {} http { server { listen 80; root /usr/share/nginx/html; index index.html; } }

24. Testing Config  |  25. Reloading

⭐ The Golden Rule

Edit Config → sudo nginx -t → If OK → sudo systemctl reload nginx

Never blindly reload. Always test syntax with nginx -t. Reloading applies changes gracefully without dropping active connections.

Changing Ports & Security Groups (29 - 31)

If you change listen 80; to listen 8080;, your website won't work immediately. Why?

Two Layers to Allow

  1. NGINX: Must listen on 8080.
  2. AWS Security Group: Must allow inbound TCP 8080 from the internet.
Internet ↓ AWS Security Group (Allows 8080?) ↓ NGINX Server (Listening on 8080?)
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 5

32 - 35. NGINX Logging

Logs are stored under /var/log/nginx/. They are critical for troubleshooting.

Log FilePurpose
access.log Records all incoming client requests (IP, time, URI, status).
error.log Records internal errors, warnings, and missing files.
Memory Trick ACCESS → Who requested what?  |  ERROR → What went wrong?

36. Hosting Multiple Websites  |  37. server_name

NGINX uses multiple server blocks and the server_name directive to host multiple websites on one server.

server { listen 80; server_name example.com; root /usr/share/nginx/html/example.com; } server { listen 80; server_name myapp.com; root /usr/share/nginx/html/myapp.com; }

DNS vs server_name

DNS routes both example.com and myapp.com to your EC2 IP.

NGINX looks at the HTTP Host header and uses server_name to pick the right block!

38 & 39. MIME Types

Browsers need to know file types to render them correctly (e.g., HTML vs CSS vs JS). You must include MIME types in your config:

include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
default_type application/octet-stream;

Without this, your CSS files might load as plain text, breaking your site's styling!

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 6

44. Custom 404 Page  |  45. try_files

Custom 404 Page

error_page 404 /404.html;

Returns a friendly HTML page instead of NGINX's default "Not Found" error.

try_files Directive

try_files $uri $uri/ =404;

Instructs NGINX to: Check for file → Check for directory → Return 404 if neither exists.

HTTPS and SSL/TLS (47 - 49)

HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) encrypts data between the client and the server, protecting sensitive information like passwords.

  • SSL vs TLS: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the modern, secure protocol. SSL is obsolete, though people still say "SSL certificate."
Browser → HTTPS :443 → NGINX (TLS decrypts) → App

50 - 53. Let's Encrypt & Certbot

Let's Encrypt is a free, automated Certificate Authority. Certbot is the tool used to fetch and renew these certs.

sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d example.com

⚠️ Standalone mode requires Port 80 to be free, meaning NGINX must temporarily be stopped.

Certificate Files

Stored in /etc/letsencrypt/live/...

  • fullchain.pem: The public cert.
  • privkey.pem: The private key. Never expose this!
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 7

54. NGINX HTTPS Config  |  56. HTTP → HTTPS Redirect

# Redirect HTTP to HTTPS server { listen 80; server_name example.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } # Secure HTTPS Server server { listen 443 ssl; server_name example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/.../fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/.../privkey.pem; root /usr/share/nginx/html/example.com; }

57 - 59. Reverse Proxy & Benefits

Instead of the client directly contacting a backend server (Node.js, Tomcat, etc.), NGINX sits in front of it.

Client → NGINX (Reverse Proxy) → Backend Server

Key Benefits

  • Security: Backend stays private
  • Load Balancing: Distribute traffic
  • Caching: Store responses
  • Centralized HTTPS: Terminate TLS once
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 8

61. proxy_pass & Headers  |  63. Security

location / { proxy_pass http://10.0.1.10:80; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; }

proxy_pass tells NGINX where to forward traffic. Headers like X-Real-IP help the backend know the original client's IP, instead of just seeing NGINX's IP.

63. Reverse Proxy Security

Never leave your backend server open to the public internet (0.0.0.0/0). Restrict its AWS Security Group to only accept traffic from the NGINX server's private IP/SG.

64. Load Balancing  |  66. upstream Block

When traffic grows, one backend server isn't enough. NGINX can distribute traffic among a group of servers using the upstream block.

upstream backend_pool { server 10.0.1.10:80; server 10.0.1.11:80; } server { location / { proxy_pass http://backend_pool; } }
Clients ↓ NGINX ↓ backend_pool / \ ↓ ↓ Web 1 Web 2
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 9

Load Balancing Algorithms & Failover (67 - 71)

Algorithm / FeatureHow it works
Round Robin (Default) Takes turns evenly. (Req1→Srv1, Req2→Srv2, Req3→Srv1)
Least Connections Sends new request to the server with the fewest active connections. Great for varying request durations.
Weighted weight=3; Higher weight = gets more traffic proportionally. Best when servers have unequal CPU/RAM.
Backup / Failover backup; Only receives traffic if the primary servers are down/unavailable. High Availability redundancy!

72 - 76. Timeouts

Tune timeouts based on your application's workload to prevent hanging connections or premature disconnects.

  • keepalive_timeout: Max idle time for a keep-alive connection.
  • proxy_connect_timeout: Max time to establish connection to backend.
  • proxy_read_timeout: Max time waiting for backend response.
  • proxy_send_timeout: Max time to send data to backend.
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 10

77 - 80. Caching

Caching stores copies of responses at the NGINX layer so future identical requests don't hit the backend. This provides faster responses and reduced backend load.

Request 1: Client → NGINX → Backend → Response → Cache at NGINX → Client Request 2: Client → NGINX Cache → Client (Backend completely skipped!)

Basic Cache Config

proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx keys_zone=my_cache:10m max_size=1g inactive=60m; server { location / { proxy_cache my_cache; proxy_pass http://backend; } }

⚠️ Warning

Do NOT cache everything blindly! Do not cache sensitive user data (like logged-in profiles or checkout pages). Incorrect caching serves the wrong data to the wrong user.

NGINX Architectures (82 - 86)

STATIC WEB SERVER Internet ↓ NGINX ↓ /usr/share/nginx/html
REVERSE PROXY Client ↓ NGINX Server ↓ Backend Server (App)
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 11

87. Troubleshooting Checklist

Site Doesn't Load?

  • Check systemctl status nginx
  • Test config nginx -t
  • AWS Security Group allows 80/443?
  • EC2 Public IP correct?

404 Error?

  • Check root path and index
  • Check try_files config
  • File permissions

CSS Not Loading?

Check include /etc/nginx/mime.types;. Hard refresh browser (Ctrl+Shift+R).

88. Best Practices

  • Always run sudo nginx -t before reloading!
  • Keep backups of nginx.conf before editing.
  • Use HTTPS for production. Protect privkey.pem.
  • Monitor access.log and error.log.
  • Keep backend servers private (only accessible by NGINX).

89. Commands Cheat Sheet

systemctl start nginx
systemctl stop nginx
systemctl restart nginx
systemctl reload nginx
systemctl status nginx
nginx -t
systemctl enable nginx
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 12

95. 🎯 Interview Questions

Q1. What is NGINX?
A high-performance web server, reverse proxy, load balancer, and caching server.
Q5. Where is the config file?
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf
Q8. What is a reverse proxy?
A server that sits in front of backend servers and forwards client requests to them.
Q9. What does proxy_pass do?
Specifies the backend destination where NGINX forwards requests.
Q11. What is round-robin?
Distributes load sequentially across backend servers.
Q18. DNS vs server_name?
DNS gets request to IP. server_name tells NGINX which config block to use.

96. Final Mental Model

INTERNET │ DOMAIN / DNS │ ↓ ┌───────────────┐ │ NGINX │ │ │ │ Web Server │ │ Reverse Proxy │ │ Load Balancer │ │ Cache / TLS │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Backend 1 Backend 2 Backend 3
🔥 One-Line Revision

NGINX receives requests, checks its config, serves static content or forwards requests to backends, providing HTTPS, load balancing, and caching.

Apache HTTPD - Handwritten Study Notes
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 1
🌐 Apache HTTPD — Part 1
Core Concepts, Installation, DNS Mapping & SSL Configuration

1. Introduction to Web Servers

What is a Web Server?

A web server is software that receives requests from clients (usually web browsers) and sends back web content such as:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
  • Images
  • Videos
  • Other static files

Communication generally happens using:

  • HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol
  • HTTPS — HTTP Secure, which uses TLS encryption

Basic Working

┌─────────────────┐ │ Client/Browser │ └────────┬────────┘ │ │ HTTP Request │ Port 80 ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Apache Web Server │ │ (HTTPD) │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ │ Fetches requested file ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Document Root │ │ /var/www/html │ └─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ HTTP Response HTML / CSS / JS

Example

When a user enters: http://example.com the browser sends a request to the web server.

Apache receives the request, finds the required content, and sends it back to the browser.

2. Local Hosting vs Production Hosting

Local File

If you open an HTML file directly from your computer:

file:///home/user/index.html

the browser is accessing the file directly from the local filesystem. This is not the same as hosting a website publicly.

Production Hosting

To make a website accessible through the Internet:

Internet↓Public IP / Domain↓Web Server↓Website Files
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 2

A server must:

  • Be connected to the Internet.
  • Have a reachable public IP or domain.
  • Run web-server software.
  • Listen on the required network ports.
  • Allow traffic through its firewall/security rules.

3. What is HTTPD?

HTTPD stands for HTTP Daemon.

  • HTTP → Hypertext Transfer Protocol
  • D → Daemon

A daemon is a background process that continuously runs and waits for incoming requests.
Apache is commonly referred to as: Apache HTTPD

Important Ports

ProtocolPortPurpose
HTTP80Normal web traffic
HTTPS443Encrypted web traffic
SSH22Remote server administration
Remember HTTP → 80  |  HTTPS → 443  |  SSH → 22

4. Apache in Production

Apache HTTPD can be used for several purposes.

4.1 Static Website Hosting

Apache can directly serve: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Images, Fonts, Videos.

/var/www/html/index.html /var/www/html/styles.css /var/www/html/logo.png

4.2 Dynamic Web Applications

Apache can work with application runtimes such as: PHP, Python, Perl. This allows Apache to serve applications rather than only static files.

4.3 Reverse Proxy

Apache can receive requests from users and forward them to backend applications.

Client │ ▼ Apache │ ├──► Node.js Application │ ├──► Flask Application │ └──► Other Backend Services
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 3

Why use a reverse proxy? It can help with: Routing, Security, SSL/TLS termination, Backend abstraction, Centralized access control.

4.4 Load Balancing

Apache can distribute requests across multiple backend servers.

┌──► Server 1 │ Client ──► Apache │ ├──► Server 2 │ └──► Server 3

This can improve: Availability, Scalability, Fault tolerance, Performance.

4.5 Virtual Hosting

A single server can host multiple websites. Example: Server IP: 203.0.113.10

example1.com ──► Website 1 example2.com ──► Website 2 example3.com ──► Website 3

This is called Virtual Hosting.

4.6 Security & Encryption

Apache can also handle: SSL/TLS certificates, Access control, Authentication, Custom error pages, Security-related configuration.

5. Setting Up Apache on AWS EC2

AWS EC2: Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual machines called instances.
For this setup, you can use: OS: Amazon Linux | Instance: t2.micro or an appropriate currently available Free Tier instance | Access: EC2 Instance Connect or SSH.

6. AWS Security Group Configuration

A Security Group acts as a virtual firewall for the EC2 instance.

Required Inbound Rules

TypePortSourcePurpose
SSH22Your IPServer administration
HTTP800.0.0.0/0Public website
HTTPS4430.0.0.0/0Secure website
Security Tip

Do not unnecessarily expose SSH (22) to: 0.0.0.0/0

Restrict SSH access to trusted IP addresses whenever possible.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 4

7. Installing Apache HTTPD

On Amazon Linux/RHEL/Fedora-based systems, the Apache package is generally called: httpd

On Debian/Ubuntu systems, it is generally: apache2

Installation Commands

# Update installed packages sudo yum update -y # Install Apache sudo yum install httpd -y # Start Apache sudo systemctl start httpd # Enable Apache at boot sudo systemctl enable httpd # Check Apache status sudo systemctl status httpd

What Each Command Does

yum update
Updates available packages.
sudo yum update -y

yum install
Installs Apache.
sudo yum install httpd -y

systemctl start
Starts the Apache service immediately.
sudo systemctl start httpd

systemctl enable
Makes Apache start automatically after reboot.
sudo systemctl enable httpd

systemctl status
Shows the current service state.
sudo systemctl status httpd

8. Linux Firewall Configuration

When running Apache on a local RHEL/CentOS-type server, the operating-system firewall may also need to allow HTTP and HTTPS.

Using firewalld:

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Important

On AWS, there can be multiple network-control layers, including:

Browser→AWS Security Group→OS Firewall→Apache→Website

Therefore, opening a port in only one place may not be sufficient.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 5

9. Test Apache Installation

After installation, find the EC2 instance's public IP. Then open:

http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>

If Apache is configured correctly, you should see its default test page. Example: http://203.0.113.10

10. Document Root

What is Document Root?

The Document Root is the directory from which Apache serves website files.

On Amazon Linux/RHEL-based Apache installations, a common default is:

/var/www/html

Example

/var/www/html │ ├── index.html ├── styles.css ├── images/ └── scripts/

When a browser requests: http://example.com/index.html
Apache can map that URL to: /var/www/html/index.html

11. Creating a Custom Website

Navigate to the Document Root: cd /var/www/html

Create an HTML file: sudo vi index.html

Example HTML

<!DOCTYPE html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <title>Production Web Server</title> <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> </head> <body> <h1>Welcome to Our Production Web Server</h1> <p>This page is served by Apache.</p> </body> </html>

Create CSS: sudo vi styles.css

body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background-color: #f4f4f4; text-align: center; padding-top: 50px; } h1 { color: #0056b3; }

Now refresh: http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>. Your custom webpage should appear.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 6

12. Apache Configuration File

The main Apache configuration file on RHEL/Amazon Linux-style installations is:

/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf

This file controls important Apache behavior.

Important Apache Directives

DirectivePurpose
ServerRootDefines Apache's main configuration/module directory
ListenSpecifies the port/IP Apache listens on
IncludeOptionalLoads additional configuration files
UserDefines the user running Apache processes
GroupDefines the group running Apache processes
DocumentRootDefines the website's root directory
DirectoryIndexDefines the default file served for a directory
ErrorLogDefines the error log
CustomLogDefines the access log

Example

ServerRoot "/etc/httpd" Listen 80 DocumentRoot "/var/www/html" DirectoryIndex index.html ErrorLog "logs/error_log" CustomLog "logs/access_log" combined

13. Understanding Important Directives

Listen
Listen 80
Tells Apache to listen for HTTP requests on port 80. For HTTPS: Listen 443

DocumentRoot
DocumentRoot "/var/www/html"
Specifies where website files are stored.

DirectoryIndex
DirectoryIndex index.html
When a user visits http://example.com/, Apache can automatically look for index.html.

ErrorLog & CustomLog
ErrorLog "logs/error_log" stores errors/warnings.
CustomLog "logs/access_log" combined records incoming client requests.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 7

14. Apache Configuration Includes

Apache supports modular configuration. For example:

IncludeOptional conf.d/*.conf

This means Apache can load additional .conf files from: /etc/httpd/conf.d/
This is useful because configurations can be separated into smaller files rather than putting everything into one large file.

15. Apache Directory Security

Apache controls access to filesystem directories using <Directory> blocks. Example:

<Directory /> AllowOverride none Require all denied </Directory>

This prevents general web access to the server's root filesystem. Then:

<Directory "/var/www/html"> Options Indexes FollowSymLinks AllowOverride None Require all granted </Directory>

allows access to the website's Document Root.

Security Principle

Operating System↓Deny by default↓Website directory↓Explicitly allow access

This is safer than allowing access to the entire filesystem.

16. MIME Types

Browsers need to know what type of content they are receiving. Apache uses MIME type mappings to associate file extensions with media types.

FileMIME Type
.htmltext/html
.csstext/css
.jstext/javascript
.pngimage/png
.jpgimage/jpeg
.jsonapplication/json

A common MIME types file is: /etc/mime.types

Apache's mod_mime module helps manage this mapping.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 8

17. Apache Logs  |  18. Access Log

Logs are extremely important for: Troubleshooting, Debugging, Security analysis, Monitoring, Understanding user requests.

On many RHEL/Amazon Linux Apache installations, logs are located under: /var/log/httpd/

There are two important logs: access_log and error_log.

Access Log

The access log records incoming requests. View it live:

sudo tail -f /var/log/httpd/access_log

Typical Combined Log Format:

<Client_IP> - - [Timestamp] "Method URI Protocol" Status_Code Bytes_Sent "Referrer" "User_Agent"

Example:

192.0.2.10 - - [13/Sep/2026:22:00:00 +0530] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 1234 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
FieldMeaning
Client IPIP address of the requester
TimestampTime of request
MethodHTTP method such as GET
URIRequested resource
Status CodeResult of request
Bytes SentResponse size
ReferrerPrevious page, if provided
User AgentBrowser/client information

19. HTTP Status Codes

CodeMeaning
200OK / Successful
301Permanent Redirect
302Temporary Redirect
400Bad Request
401Unauthorized
403Forbidden
404Not Found
500Internal Server Error
502Bad Gateway
503Service Unavailable
Easy Memory Trick
  • 2xx → Success
  • 3xx → Redirect
  • 4xx → Client-side/request problem
  • 5xx → Server-side problem
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 9

20. Error Log

The error log records problems such as: Configuration errors, Startup problems, Permission issues, Module problems, Runtime warnings.

View the last 50 lines: sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/httpd/error_log

Real-Time Monitoring: sudo tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log

21. Domain Name  |  22. What is DNS?

A public IP address works, but users generally prefer a domain name. Instead of http://203.0.113.10 we want http://myexamplewebsite.xyz.

DNS = Domain Name System. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.

myexamplewebsite.xyz │ ▼ DNS (A Record) │ ▼ EC2 Public IP │ ▼ Apache Web Server

23. DNS A Record  |  24. DNS Configuration Steps

An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address.

Example Records

HostTypeValue
@AEC2 Public IP
wwwAEC2 Public IP

@ generally represents the root/apex domain (myexamplewebsite.xyz).

Configuration Steps

  1. Open DNS Management (GoDaddy, Route 53, etc.)
  2. Create A Record for root (@) to IP.
  3. Create A Record for www to IP.
  4. Verify DNS using: dig +short myexamplewebsite.xyz

25. DNS Propagation

DNS changes may not become visible everywhere immediately. Propagation time varies by TTL, caching, and resolvers. Don't assume a DNS change is broken simply because it doesn't appear instantly.

SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 10

26. HTTPS & SSL/TLS

HTTP traffic can be observed or modified more easily than properly encrypted HTTPS traffic. HTTPS uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) to provide: Encryption, Integrity, and Server authentication.

HTTP

Browser ──► Server

Unencrypted traffic (Port 80)

HTTPS

Browser ══► Server

Encrypted TLS connection (Port 443)

Let's Encrypt & Certbot (27 - 30)

Let's Encrypt provides publicly trusted TLS certificates.
Certbot is a tool that obtains/manages certificates using the ACME protocol.

28. Install: sudo yum install certbot python3-certbot-apache -y

29. Obtain Certificate: Standalone mode temporarily uses port 80. Stop Apache first!

sudo systemctl stop httpd
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d myexamplewebsite.xyz

30. Certificate Files

Stored in: /etc/letsencrypt/live/...

  • fullchain.pem → Public cert chain
  • privkey.pem → Private key (Secret!)

⚠️ Never expose or share the private key.

31. Configuring HTTPS in Apache

Apache can be configured to listen on port 443.

Listen 443 <VirtualHost *:443> ServerName myexamplewebsite.xyz DocumentRoot /var/www/html SSLEngine on SSLCertificateFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/myexamplewebsite.xyz/fullchain.pem SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/myexamplewebsite.xyz/privkey.pem ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/ssl_error_log CustomLog /var/log/httpd/ssl_access_log combined </VirtualHost>
SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION & DEVOPS // STUDY NOTES PAGE 11

32. Understanding <VirtualHost>

A VirtualHost defines how Apache should handle requests for a particular host/domain.

<VirtualHost *:443>
ServerName myexamplewebsite.xyz
</VirtualHost>

Meaning: Handle HTTPS requests for myexamplewebsite.xyz on port 443. This becomes especially useful when hosting multiple domains on one server.

33. Validate Apache Config  |  34. Reload vs Restart

Before restarting/reloading, check syntax:

sudo httpd -t

Expected result: Syntax OK

Why? A mistake can prevent Apache from starting.

Restart:

Stops and starts the service. (systemctl restart)

Reload:

Reloads config while keeping service running. (systemctl reload)

Custom 404 Error Page (36 - 39)

404 Not Found means the requested resource could not be found. Apache returns a default page, but you can customize it.

Step 1: Create the HTML page:

sudo vi /var/www/html/error_404.html

Step 2: Configure httpd.conf:

ErrorDocument 404 /error_404.html

Step 3: Apply

httpd -t→reload→test bad URL

Apache will now serve the custom HTML file instead of the default error message.
